advances: For every positive-volume integer fiber, this theorem converts ordered minimum reflection mass and its actual weighted logarithmic loss into a lower bound for the canonical reflected midpoint measure, then lifts that bound at the same point to mixed-integer depth. The entropy is bounded by the intrinsic rank of the positive lattice displacements in the base, independently of the continuous dimension and without a hypothesis on midpoint centroids. The actual entropy bound is retained for choosing the base fiber. A uniform joint mass/entropy selection inequality would imply the locked conjecture, but that selection inequality is not proved here.

external_sources:
R. J. Gardner, [The Brunn-Minkowski Inequality](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-02-00941-2), Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 39 (2002), pages 355 to 405, Theorem 4.1, printed page 362; [accessible copy of the published article](https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/COURSES/520s/523/HO.523.20/Gardner.BullAMS.02.pdf). The exact form used is: if \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^d\) are nonempty bounded measurable sets, \(0<\theta<1\), and their weighted Minkowski sum is measurable, then \(\operatorname{vol}_d((1-\theta)A+\theta B)^{1/d}\ge(1-\theta)\operatorname{vol}_d(A)^{1/d}+\theta\operatorname{vol}_d(B)^{1/d}\). Our applications use positive-volume fibers or positive-volume reflected intersections. These are compact convex sets, so their Minkowski sums are compact and measurable. The necessary containments follow from convexity of \(C\) and were proved above. Empty or zero-volume intersections are handled without applying the theorem.

Laszlo Lovasz and Santosh Vempala, [The Geometry of Logconcave Functions and Sampling Algorithms](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~vempala/papers/logcon.pdf), Theorem 5.1, printed page 14 of the author manuscript; [journal DOI: 10.1002/rsa.20135](https://doi.org/10.1002/rsa.20135). The portion used states that convolution preserves log-concavity for two log-concave functions. We apply it only to the two integrable uniform probability densities \(w_j^{-1}\mathbf{1}_{C_j}\). Rescaling their convolution gives \(f_0\); compact support gives its finite first moment. The mixture itself need not be log-concave. Its depth bound is supplied by the declared accepted predecessor `5bd39b316ef3c194`, not by an additional external entropy theorem.
proof:
Compactness of the projection of \(C\) onto \(\mathbb R^n\) implies that it contains only finitely many lattice points. Thus all lattice sums and representative sets in the statement are finite. Positive-volume fibers are full-dimensional compact convex bodies in \(\mathbb R^d\); no probability measure is assigned to a zero-volume fiber. Fix a positive-volume integer fiber \(j\) for the remainder of the argument.

First we bound its actual logarithmic loss. Convexity gives \((1-\theta)C_z+\theta C_{z'}\subseteq C_{(1-\theta)z+\theta z'}\) for real base points and \(0<\theta<1\). When the two fibers have positive volume, the Brunn-Minkowski inequality therefore gives

\[
w_{(1-\theta)z+\theta z'}^{1/d}
\ge(1-\theta)w_z^{1/d}+\theta w_{z'}^{1/d}.
\]

In particular, the positive-fiber domain is convex. Its common reflected domain \(\mathcal D:=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:w_{j+v}w_{j-v}>0\}\) is convex, symmetric about zero, and contains zero. The function \(b(v):=\min\{w_{j+v}^{1/d},w_{j-v}^{1/d}\}\) is positive, even, and concave on \(\mathcal D\). Indeed, each of its two defining functions is concave there, and the minimum of their two concavity bounds is at least the corresponding convex combination of their pointwise minima. Evenness and concavity imply \(b(v)\le b(0)\).

Define \(\phi(v):=d\log(b(0)/b(v))\) on \(\mathcal D\). Since negative logarithm is convex and decreasing, its composition with the positive concave function \(b\) is convex. Thus \(\phi\) is even, convex, and nonnegative, with \(\phi(0)=0\). At every \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), \(\phi(v)=\log(w_j/\alpha(v))\). This proves, in particular, \(\alpha(v)\le w_j\) and \(E_j\ge0\).

Let \(V:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\mathcal U_j\) and \(L:=V\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Because \(V\) is spanned by integer vectors, \(L\) is a lattice of rank \(r_j\) in \(V\). In lattice coordinates, \(L/5L\) has exactly \(5^{r_j}\) classes. Also \(\mathcal D\cap L=\mathcal U_j\), because \(\mathcal D\cap\mathbb Z^n=\mathcal U_j\subseteq V\).

For \(t\ge0\), put \(N(t):=\#\{v\in\mathcal U_j:\phi(v)\le t\}\). The set counted is finite and contains zero. Partition it into its classes modulo \(5L\), and choose a largest class and a point \(v_0\) in that class. For each \(v\) in the same class, \((v-v_0)/5\in L\), and

\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi\!\left(\frac{v-v_0}{5}\right)
&=\phi\!\left(\frac15v+\frac15(-v_0)+\frac35\,0\right)\\
&\le\frac15\phi(v)+\frac15\phi(-v_0)+\frac35\phi(0)
\le\frac{2t}{5}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The convex combination lies in \(\mathcal D\), and this map is injective. Its image is therefore counted by \(N(2t/5)\). The largest class contains at least \(N(t)/5^{r_j}\) points, proving \(N(t)\le5^{r_j}N(2t/5)\).

For \(s>0\), set \(Z(s):=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}e^{-s\phi(v)}\). Integrating \(s e^{-st}\) from \(\phi(v)\) to infinity for each of the finitely many points gives \(Z(s)=s\int_0^\infty e^{-st}N(t)\,dt\). The counting bound and the substitution \(u=2t/5\) give

\[
\begin{aligned}
Z(2/5)
&=\frac25\int_0^\infty e^{-2t/5}N(t)\,dt\\
&\le5^{r_j}\frac25\int_0^\infty e^{-2t/5}N(2t/5)\,dt
=5^{r_j}Z(1).
\end{aligned}
\]

Write \(\pi_v:=\alpha(v)/S_j\) for \(v\in\mathcal U_j\). These are probability weights, and \(Z(1)=S_j/w_j\). Jensen's inequality now yields

\[
\exp(3E_j/5)
\le\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\pi_v e^{3\phi(v)/5}
=\frac{Z(2/5)}{Z(1)}
\le5^{r_j}.
\]

Taking logarithms proves \(E_j\le(5\log5/3)r_j\). If \(r_j=0\), then \(\mathcal U_j=\{0\}\), \(L=\{0\}\), and \(N(t)=Z(s)=1\) for \(t\ge0\), \(s>0\). Thus the same argument includes this case and gives \(E_j=0\) exactly.

We next compare all midpoint densities with the central midpoint density. For \(v\in\mathcal U_j\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), put \(R_v(x):=C_{j+v}\cap(2x-C_{j-v})\). The convolution formula for independent uniform points, followed by scaling their sum by one half, gives the probability density

\[
f_v(x)=\frac{2^d}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}\operatorname{vol}_d R_v(x)
=\frac{2^d}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbf{1}_{C_{j+v}}(y)\mathbf{1}_{C_{j-v}}(2x-y)\,dy.
\]

Every \(f_v\) is continuous. To see this directly, the boundary of a positive-volume compact convex body has Lebesgue measure zero: contraction by a factor \(1-\varepsilon\) about an interior point lies in its interior, and the difference between the body and this contraction has volume \([1-(1-\varepsilon)^d]\) times the body's volume, tending to zero. If \(x_k\to x\), the second indicator in the integral therefore converges for almost every \(y\), and the first indicator is an integrable dominating function. Dominated convergence proves continuity. Convexity of \(C\) also gives \((C_{j+v}+C_{j-v})/2\subseteq C_j\); hence \(f_v\) is compactly supported in \(C_j\).

For each \(x\), reflection gives \(R_{-v}(x)=2x-R_v(x)\), so these two sets have equal volume. If \(p\in R_v(x)\) and \(q\in R_{-v}(x)\), then \(p\in C_{j+v}\), \(q\in C_{j-v}\), \(2x-p\in C_{j-v}\), and \(2x-q\in C_{j+v}\). Consequently both \((p+q)/2\) and \(2x-(p+q)/2\) belong to \(C_j\). This proves

\[
\frac{R_v(x)+R_{-v}(x)}2
\subseteq R_0(x)=C_j\cap(2x-C_j).
\]

If \(R_v(x)\) has positive volume, Brunn-Minkowski applied to the two reflected compact convex sets gives \(\operatorname{vol}_d R_0(x)\ge\operatorname{vol}_d R_v(x)\). If \(R_v(x)\) is empty or has zero volume, this volume inequality holds without invoking Brunn-Minkowski. The density formula thus gives, for all \(x\),

\[
f_v(x)
\le\frac{w_j^2}{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}f_0(x)
\le\left(\frac{w_j}{\alpha(v)}\right)^2 f_0(x)
=e^{2\phi(v)}f_0(x).
\]

It follows that \(\nu_v\ll\nu_0\), with density ratio at most \(e^{2\phi(v)}\). The negative part of the relative-entropy integrand is integrable, since \(t\log t\ge-1/e\) for \(t\ge0\), with \(0\log0=0\), and the reference is a probability measure. The upper ratio bound also makes the positive part integrable and gives \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\nu_v\|\nu_0)\le2\phi(v)\).

Define the probability measure \(\widetilde P_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\pi_v\nu_v\). It has continuous density \(\sum_v\pi_v f_v\), compactly supported in \(C_j\), and is absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu_0\). Convexity of \(t\log t\), applied pointwise to the finite mixture of the density ratios relative to \(\nu_0\) and then integrated, proves

\[
D_j:=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widetilde P_j\|\nu_0)
\le\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\pi_v D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\nu_v\|\nu_0)
\le2\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\pi_v\phi(v)
=2E_j<\infty.
\]

The normalized indicator \(w_j^{-1}\mathbf{1}_{C_j}\) is log-concave. Theorem 5.1 of Lovasz and Vempala, stated in EXTERNAL SOURCES, shows that its convolution with itself is log-concave. Positive scaling of the variable and of the density preserves log-concavity, so the density \(f_0\) of the central midpoint law is log-concave. That law is supported in the compact set \(C_j\), hence has a finite first absolute moment.

Apply accepted fact `5bd39b316ef3c194` with its \(P=\widetilde P_j\), \(Q=\nu_0\), \(f=\sum_v\pi_v f_v\), \(g=f_0\), and \(D=D_j\). We have checked continuity and compact support of \(f\), log-concavity and finite first moment of \(g\), absolute continuity, and finite relative entropy. That fact supplies a point \(x_j^\star\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}\widetilde P_j)\subseteq C_j\) for which

\[
\operatorname{TD}_{\widetilde P_j}(x_j^\star)
\ge\frac{\ell}{8(D_j+\log2)}
\ge\frac{\ell}{8(2E_j+\log2)}.
\]

To pass from this probability measure to \(\kappa_j\), put \(\sigma_j:=(S_j/2)\widetilde P_j\). Evenness of \(\alpha\) and the equality \(\nu_v=\nu_{-v}\) give the exact identity \(\sigma_j=(w_j/2)\nu_0+\sum_{v\in\mathcal R_j}\alpha(v)\nu_v\). For any closed halfspace \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), if the midpoint of two points is in \(G\), at least one endpoint is in \(G\). For independent \(X,X'\sim\lambda_j\), the union bound therefore gives

\[
\nu_0(G)
=\mathbb P((X+X')/2\in G)
\le\mathbb P(X\in G\text{ or }X'\in G)
\le2\lambda_j(G).
\]

The assertion includes equality on the boundary because \(G\) is closed. Comparing the central terms and retaining the identical noncentral terms proves \(\sigma_j(G)\le\kappa_j(G)\) for every closed halfspace. This is a halfspace comparison; no domination on arbitrary Borel sets is asserted or used. Taking infima over the same halfspaces at any \(x\) yields \(\operatorname{TD}_{\kappa_j}(x)\ge(S_j/2)\operatorname{TD}_{\widetilde P_j}(x)\). At the point supplied by the accepted relative-entropy lemma, we obtain

\[
\operatorname{TD}_{\kappa_j}(x_j^\star)
\ge\frac{S_j}{2}\operatorname{TD}_{\widetilde P_j}(x_j^\star)
\ge\frac{\ell S_j}{16(2E_j+\log2)}.
\]

We now use the pointwise lifting in the proof of accepted fact `15ec168ab4433041`, equations (7) through (11), with the exact substitutions \(m=j\), \(y=x\), \(a=a_H\), \(b=b_H\), and \(\alpha_v=\alpha(v)\) on \(\mathcal R_j\). Explicitly, for any \(x\in C_j\) and any proper ambient halfspace through \((j,x)\), write

\[
H=\{(z,u):a_H^\top(z-j)+b_H^\top(u-x)\ge0\},
\qquad (a_H,b_H)\ne(0,0).
\]

If \(b_H\ne0\), put \(G:=\{u:b_H^\top(u-x)\ge0\}\); if \(b_H=0\), put \(G:=\mathbb R^d\). The predecessor's inequality (11) gives \(\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\ge\kappa_j(G)\ge\operatorname{TD}_{\kappa_j}(x)\). In particular, when \(b_H=0\), its equation (9) charges the whole central fiber on the ambient boundary, so this argument does not assume that vertical ambient hyperplanes have zero mixed mass. Every proper closed halfspace containing \((j,x)\) contains a parallel halfspace through that point, so the same bound holds for all such halfspaces. If the whole ambient space is admitted, its mass is \(W\), while \(\Lambda_j\le S_j\le W\): the first inequality follows from \(S_j\ge w_j\), and the second from \(\alpha(v)\le w_{j+v}\) and reindexing the finite sum. Thus the whole-space case also has the required mass. Taking the infimum proves \(h_S((j,x))\ge\operatorname{TD}_{\kappa_j}(x)\) for every \(x\in C_j\), in particular for the same \(x_j^\star\) selected above.

Finally, the ordered sum contains the central term once and every noncentral unordered pair twice, so \(S_j=w_j+2\sum_{v\in\mathcal R_j}\alpha(v)\) and \(\Lambda_j=(S_j+w_j)/2\le S_j\). Since \(E_j\le\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}}r_j\) and \(\log2\le2\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}}\),

\[
\frac{\ell S_j}{16(2E_j+\log2)}
\ge\frac{\ell\Lambda_j}{16(2\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}}r_j+\log2)}
\ge\frac{\ell}{32\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}}}\frac{\Lambda_j}{r_j+1}.
\]

This includes \(r_j=0\), when \(S_j=\Lambda_j=w_j\), \(E_j=0\), and \(\kappa_j=w_j\lambda_j\). The rank bound concerns only \(\mathcal U_j\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\); no dimension statement about midpoint centroids has been used.

Because \(2E_j+\log2\le2(1+E_j)\), the depth at \((j,x_j^\star)\) is at least \((\ell/32)S_j/(1+E_j)\). There are finitely many positive-volume integer fibers, so choose a \(j\) maximizing this ratio to obtain the stated point \(p^\star\). Under the additional uniform selection inequality in the statement, this point has depth at least \((a\ell/32)2^{-n}W\). Replacing the constant by \(\min\{a\ell/32,1/(2e)\}\) places it strictly between zero and \(1/e\), as required by the locked problem. Bodies with \(W=0\) already satisfy that problem at any point of the nonempty mixed set. The uniform selection inequality is the unproved hypothesis of this last implication, not a consequence of the rank estimate.
statement:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body. For every real base point \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), put \(C_z:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:(z,x)\in C\}\) and \(w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\), with zero volume for empty or lower-dimensional fibers. Suppose \(W:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}w_z>0\). Keep the canonical mixed set \(S:=C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\), and define \(h_S(p):=\inf_{H\ni p}\mathcal H_d(S\cap H)\), where the infimum is over closed ambient halfspaces. For every \(z\) with \(w_z>0\), \(\lambda_z\) denotes the uniform probability measure on \(C_z\), not its unnormalized volume measure. These are the objects of accepted fact `15ec168ab4433041`, with the fiber notation extended to real base points.

Fix \(j\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(w_j>0\). For every oriented lattice displacement \(v\in\mathbb Z^n\), define \(\alpha(v):=\min\{w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\}\), and put \(\mathcal U_j:=\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:\alpha(v)>0\}\). In particular, \(0\in\mathcal U_j\) and \(\alpha(0)=w_j\). For \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), let \(\nu_v\) be the law of \((X^++X^-)/2\) for independent \(X^+\sim\lambda_{j+v}\) and \(X^-\sim\lambda_{j-v}\). For \(v=0\), the two variables are independent copies from \(\lambda_j\). Thus \(\nu_v=\nu_{-v}\).

Let \(\mathcal R_j\) contain one representative of each unordered pair \(\{v,-v\}\) in \(\mathcal U_j\setminus\{0\}\), and retain the canonical measure

\[
\kappa_j:=w_j\lambda_j+\sum_{v\in\mathcal R_j}\alpha(v)\nu_v.
\]

This is exactly \(\kappa_m\) of accepted fact `15ec168ab4433041` at \(m=j\): its representative set is \(\mathcal R_j\), its coefficient \(\alpha_v\) equals \(\alpha(v)\) on that set, and its midpoint pushforward \(M_\#(\lambda_{j+v}\otimes\lambda_{j-v})\), with \(M(x,x')=(x+x')/2\), is \(\nu_v\).

Define the ordered reflection mass \(S_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\alpha(v)\) and the scalar total mass \(\Lambda_j:=|\kappa_j|=(S_j+w_j)/2\). The scalar \(\Lambda_j\) is precisely \(P_m\) in equation (12) of accepted fact `15ec168ab4433041` at \(m=j\); \(S_j\) is not the mixed set \(S\). With natural logarithms, define

\[
E_j:=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j}\frac{\alpha(v)}{S_j}\log\frac{w_j}{\alpha(v)},
\qquad
r_j:=\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\mathcal U_j.
\]

The rank \(r_j\) is a rank of base displacements, not a rank of midpoint centroids. For a finite Borel measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), write \(\operatorname{TD}_\mu(x):=\inf_{G\ni x}\mu(G)\), where \(G\) ranges over proper closed halfspaces in \(\mathbb R^d\). This is \(D_\mu(x)\) in accepted fact `15ec168ab4433041`, so \(\operatorname{HD}(\mu)=\sup_x\operatorname{TD}_\mu(x)\). Allowing the whole space among the halfspaces does not change this infimum.

Put \(\ell:=-\log(1-e^{-1})\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}}:=5\log5/3\), and \(c_\star:=\ell/(32\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}})=3\ell/(160\log5)\). Then \(0\le E_j\le\kappa_{\mathrm{ent}}r_j\), with \(0\le r_j\le n\), and there exists \(x_j^\star\in C_j\) such that

\[
\begin{aligned}
h_S((j,x_j^\star))
&\ge\operatorname{TD}_{\kappa_j}(x_j^\star)\\
&\ge\frac{\ell S_j}{16(2E_j+\log2)}
\ge c_\star\frac{\Lambda_j}{r_j+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

In particular, there exists \(p^\star\in S\) satisfying

\[
h_S(p^\star)\ge\frac{\ell}{32}
\max_{\substack{j\in\mathbb Z^n\\w_j>0}}
\frac{S_j}{1+E_j}.
\]

Consequently, a uniform inequality \(\max_{j:w_j>0}S_j/(1+E_j)\ge a\,2^{-n}W\) for some absolute \(a>0\), over all the stated bodies and dimensions, would imply the locked weak Oertel conjecture with \(c_0:=\min\{a\ell/32,1/(2e)\}\). No such uniform selection inequality is asserted here.
